messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 62, Rafael had built a life around precision. He was a married surgeon, accustomed to steady hands, long hours, and the confidence that he could keep danger at a distance by anticipating it. That certainty shattered on a late afternoon drive home when a car was struck at an intersection with such force that the metal crumpled and folded in front of him. Rafael was close enough to smell the burnt rubber and see the awkward bend of the frame, close enough that the shock of impact seemed to go through his own chest. In the days that followed, the scene did not stay in the past in the way ordinary memories did. Rafael said the memory felt “more real than normal,” vivid in a way that made everyday recollections seem thin beside it. It would force its way into his mind while he was scrubbing in, while he was eating dinner, while he was trying to fall asleep; and even when he tried to hold it in mind long enough to understand it, he found himself pushing it away before he could fully recall it, as if the details were too dangerous to let settle.

What stayed with him most were the instant, bodily impressions: the specific rough texture of the car’s torn interior, the way the damaged upholstery scraped under his fingers, the sight of cars hit by accident with their fronts collapsed or doors crushed in. Those images could arrive uninvited when he passed a collision on the freeway, and they made the original event feel close enough to touch. He also became sharply reactive to related people, especially anyone who had been in the car with him that day or who reminded him of the passengers he had feared might be injured. A familiar voice calling from the driveway, a coworker describing a family member’s fender-bender, even a patient talking casually about an accident could pull him back toward that moment. Because the memory was so vivid and because reminders appeared so easily, Rafael began organizing his days around not encountering them. He gave up pleasant activities he and his wife used to enjoy, declining dinners out and weekend drives. He avoided physical stress, turning down extra hospital cases that would keep him on his feet too long or require rapid movement through crowded spaces. He also avoided thinking about the event, refusing himself the effort of replaying it because he feared that once he started, the images would flood in and stay.

Over time, those habits narrowed his life and changed the settings in which the reminders found him. At work, the operating room had once been his place of mastery, but now the stress of long procedures and the pressure in his body made him more vulnerable to the same tightened, crash-like feeling he associated with that afternoon. Around colleagues and relatives, he became less tolerant of stories or updates involving accidents, and because he had stopped attending social gatherings and family outings he used to enjoy, every unexpected mention of a wreck from a friend or patient landed harder. The less he allowed himself to think about the crash, the less he felt he could hold it in a controlled way; instead, the memory kept breaking through in fragments, which only made him more determined not to touch it. In turn, his shrinking routine gave the traumatic scene more space in his mind. Cars hit by accident became harder to dismiss because he was scanning for them without meaning to, and a known person connected to the event could now set off a wave of unease before he had even named why. By the time he finally sought help, Rafael was exhausted by the narrowness of his world. He was still functioning as a surgeon, but he felt he was living on borrowed concentration, afraid that if he kept avoiding enjoyment, effort, and the memory itself, he would lose not only his ease but his place in his marriage and work. What brought him in was the fear that he could no longer keep these intrusions contained, and the hope that he might learn how to face the memory without it taking over every part of his day.
